claims.statement: The Met places Villanovan culture approximately between 900 and 500 BCE and identifies it as a predecessor of Etruscan culture.

value.text: The Met places Villanovan culture approximately between 900 and 500 BCE and identifies it as a predecessor of Etruscan culture.

claims.statement: The Met describes an identifiable Etruscan language around 700 BCE and cultural flourishing through the end of the second century BCE.

value.text: The Met describes an identifiable Etruscan language around 700 BCE and cultural flourishing through the end of the second century BCE.

claims.statement: Metal-rich Etruria supported skilled bronze workers whose products circulated around the Mediterranean.

value.text: Metal-rich Etruria supported skilled bronze workers whose products circulated around the Mediterranean.

claims.statement: The Met dates the Parthian imperial era to 247 BCE–224 CE.

value.text: The Met dates the Parthian imperial era to 247 BCE–224 CE.

claims.statement: Trade supported patronage of sculpture, metalwork, jewellery and ceramics, combining Hellenistic and earlier Near Eastern traditions.

value.text: Trade supported patronage of sculpture, metalwork, jewellery and ceramics, combining Hellenistic and earlier Near Eastern traditions.

claims.statement: The Met gives Mithridates I’s reign as approximately 171–138 BCE.

value.text: The Met gives Mithridates I’s reign as approximately 171–138 BCE.

claims.statement: The Met dates settlement at Jenne-jeno to the third century BCE, with its archaeological sequence beginning around 250 BCE.

value.text: The Met dates settlement at Jenne-jeno to the third century BCE, with its archaeological sequence beginning around 250 BCE.

claims.statement: The settlement occupied the fertile Middle Niger floodplain in what is now Mali.

value.text: The settlement occupied the fertile Middle Niger floodplain in what is now Mali.

claims.statement: UNESCO describes the Aksumite kingdom in northern Ethiopia across the first to eighth centuries CE.

value.text: UNESCO describes the Aksumite kingdom in northern Ethiopia across the first to eighth centuries CE.

claims.statement: Its exchange networks linked inland northeastern Africa with the Red Sea through the port of Adulis.

value.text: Its exchange networks linked inland northeastern Africa with the Red Sea through the port of Adulis.

claims.statement: The map uses UNESCO’s reference position for Aksum and Red Sea exchange, not a territorial boundary.
UNESCO identifies Sanchi as a major Buddhist sanctuary from the third century BCE through the first century CE.

value.text: UNESCO identifies Sanchi as a major Buddhist sanctuary from the third century BCE through the first century CE.

claims.statement: Ashoka’s pillar and a brick stupa were followed by enlargement and ornamentation under later dynasties.

value.text: Ashoka’s pillar and a brick stupa were followed by enlargement and ornamentation under later dynasties.

claims.statement: The map uses UNESCO’s reference position for Early Buddhist Sanchi, not a territorial boundary.
The Met describes Scythian migration to the northern Black Sea region in the late eighth century BCE and substantial replacement by Sarmatian groups by the late second century BCE.

value.text: The Met describes Scythian migration to the northern Black Sea region in the late eighth century BCE and substantial replacement by Sarmatian groups by the late second century BCE.

claims.statement: Politically diverse pastoral horse-riding communities traded and interacted with neighbouring Greek settlements.

value.text: Politically diverse pastoral horse-riding communities traded and interacted with neighbouring Greek settlements.
